title: Access information in order to respond to client enquiries in a financial services environment

lessons.title: Understanding client enquiries at a grain business
lessons.html:
Grain handling is also a financial service

When a farmer delivers maize, wheat or soybeans to a silo, the grain becomes a valuable asset. The silo company records it on the client's account, may issue a silo certificate or receipt, charges storage and handling fees, and may pay out the farmer or a buyer when the grain is sold. Some clients use stored grain as security for finance. This makes the office at a silo or grain cooperative a financial services environment, and client enquiries must be handled accurately and carefully.

Typical enquiries

  • How many tons do I have in storage, and at which silo?
  • What grade did my last delivery get, and why?
  • What are the storage, handling and drying costs on my account?
  • When will my payment be made, and has it been paid?
  • Can I transfer grain to a buyer, and what documents are needed?
  • Why was a deduction made for moisture or foreign matter?

Identify what the client really needs

Listen carefully and ask questions to clarify the enquiry. A farmer who asks "Where is my money?" may need the payment status, the reason for a delay or details of a deduction. Write down the key facts: client name, account or client number, delivery or contract number, dates and the exact question.

Confirm identity first

Before you give any account information, confirm that you are speaking to the account holder or a person authorised on the account. Use your company's verification steps, for example checking the client number, ID details or authorised signatory list. Never give account details to someone who cannot be verified, even if they say they are a family member or the farm manager.

Know your limits

Some questions are outside your authority, for example requests for advice on whether to sell now or later, or disputes about grading. Know who in the business handles these and refer the client correctly.

lessons.title: Finding and checking the information
lessons.html:
Sources of information

To answer an enquiry you need to find the correct, current information. Common sources in a grain business are:

SourceWhat it tells you
Client account systemStock balances, transactions, fees, payments
Weighbridge and intake recordsDelivery dates, gross and net mass, truck details
Grading certificatesGrade, moisture, defects, deductions
Contracts and transfer documentsSale terms, buyer details, transfer status
Tariff scheduleCurrent storage and handling rates
Policies and proceduresWhat the company allows and how to process requests

Accessing information properly

  • Use only your own login and only for work purposes.
  • Look up only the accounts you need for the enquiry.
  • Never share passwords or leave a screen open when you walk away.
  • Do not print or email client information unless it is necessary and allowed.

Client information is personal information protected by the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA). Misusing it can harm the client and expose the business to penalties.

Check before you answer

Information must be accurate. Cross-check figures: does the stock balance agree with the intake records less withdrawals and transfers? Is the tariff you are quoting the current one? Is the payment shown as approved or actually paid? If information seems wrong or incomplete, do not guess. Tell the client you will confirm and get back to them, and then raise it with the responsible person.

Interpreting the information

Make sure you understand what you are reading. For example, net mass after grading deductions is not the same as the weighbridge gross mass, and a payment that is approved may still take time to reach the client's bank account. Explain these differences in plain language.

lessons.title: Responding and following up
lessons.html:
Give a clear, correct response

Once you have the information, respond in a way the client can understand and act on.

  1. Restate the question to show you understood it.
  2. Give the facts clearly: numbers, dates, reference numbers.
  3. Explain any terms or deductions in simple words.
  4. Tell the client what happens next and by when.
  5. Check that the client is satisfied or has further questions.

Choosing the channel

Simple balance enquiries may be answered by phone after verification. Detailed statements, transfer confirmations or anything the client will rely on for finance should be given in writing, using the company's approved format. Send written information only to verified contact details on record.

When you cannot answer immediately

Be honest. Say what you are doing to find out and give a realistic time for your reply. Record the enquiry in the query log or system, refer it to the right person and follow up to make sure the client gets an answer. A promise to call back that is not kept damages trust quickly.

Recording the enquiry

Record each enquiry: date, client, question, information given, who handled it and the outcome. This protects you and the business if there is a later dispute and helps identify common problems, such as confusion about drying charges.

Professional conduct

  • Treat all clients equally and respectfully, large or small producers.
  • Do not give investment or market advice unless you are authorised to do so.
  • Do not discuss one client's information with another client.
  • Escalate complaints according to the complaints procedure.

Key points

  • Verify the client's identity before giving any account information.
  • Use the correct, current sources and cross-check figures before answering.
  • Protect client information in line with POPIA and company policy.
  • Explain answers in plain language and confirm what happens next.
  • Record every enquiry and follow up on anything you could not answer immediately.
